Pulling Up Seedlings: Why Does Helping Growth So Easily Replace It?
A man in the state of Song worried that the seedlings in his field were growing too slowly.
He did not sit around waiting.
He went into the field and pulled each seedling upward, one by one. When he had finished, he returned home exhausted and told his family:
“What a tiring day. I've helped the seedlings grow taller.”
His son hurried to the field and found that all the seedlings had withered.
The story is often reduced to a single lesson:
Do not be impatient. More haste, less speed.
There is nothing wrong with that.
But the farmer in the story did more than “get too impatient.”
He really did make every seedling a little taller, immediately.
At least if you measured from the ground to the tip of each leaf, he had achieved a result. What he had destroyed was the part the seedlings needed in order to keep growing.
The fable therefore first forces us to distinguish two things we easily confuse:
**Making growth look as though it has happened is not the same as enabling a being to keep growing.**
Why did the farmer pull up the seedlings?
Because growth was too slow, and too unwilling to take orders.

After sowing, he could water, weed, and watch the weather, but he could not directly command the roots to grow a little more today. The seedlings absorbed nutrients and unfolded through processes of their own. Many changes took place underground, without immediately giving the person tending them a result he could verify.
That kind of waiting is unsettling.
I have put in the time. Why can't I see any progress?
I have explained the method. Why haven't they learned it yet?
I have provided the opportunity. Why hasn't the change arrived on schedule?
When the helper is more impatient than the person being helped, it is all too easy to mistake the helper's timetable for the timetable of growth itself.
Unable to make the seedlings truly grow faster, the farmer changed the most visible measure.
The seedlings were taller.
They just could not go on living.
Many attempts to “help someone grow” quietly begin to pursue this kind of visible height.
Before someone has developed an understanding of their own, we arrange a set of standard answers for them.
Before they can complete a task independently, we do every crucial part ourselves and leave them only to hand in the result.
While they are still exploring what matters to them, we prematurely turn an interest into a plan, an identity, or a future path.
All these approaches can improve performance at once.
The answers look tidier, progress becomes steadier, and the results are easier to assess.
The helper gains a feeling of certainty: at last, things are moving forward.

But if every difficulty is removed in advance by someone else, every problem defined on their behalf, and every direction arranged before it has begun to take shape, the person may acquire only a better record of completion, not a greater capacity to grow.
The farmer performed the act of “getting taller” for the seedlings.
And precisely because he did, the seedlings could never again perform it for themselves.
Yet after telling this story, the Mencius does not give “Do nothing” as the correct answer.

It immediately observes that few people in the world refrain from trying to help seedlings grow. Some think tending them is useless, so they abandon them without even weeding. Others, like the man from Song, pull them upward. The first neglect their duty of care; the second do not merely fail to help, but cause harm.
This context matters.
It places two opposite mistakes side by side:
Abandoning care.
Replacing growth.
The farmer cannot grow on behalf of the seedlings, but that does not mean the seedlings have no need of him.

The soil can be prepared, weeds removed, water supplied, and outside harm kept away. External conditions cannot create the life within a root, but they can determine whether that root still has a chance to do its work.
The real question has therefore never been:
Should we intervene?
It is:
**Does this intervention provide conditions for the other person's own growth, or replace that growth with results we can control?**
The boundary is not always easy to see.
Growth does require demands, practice, and limits.

Someone attempting something difficult for the first time may not persist of their own accord. A skill often develops only through repetition, correction, and temporary discomfort. If we call every outside demand “pulling up seedlings,” care deteriorates into spectatorship.
Sometimes the helper has to say:
“You still need to practice this step.”
“Someone else cannot bear this consequence for you.”
“What you are doing does not yet meet the standards we share.”
These judgments do not necessarily amount to forcing growth.
The difference lies in whose ability the demands ultimately increase.
If practice gradually enables someone to judge and complete things independently, while reducing their dependence on a supervisor, outside pressure may be becoming a support for growth.
If practice merely makes them better at guessing what an evaluator wants to see, and they cannot continue once supervision disappears, what we have trained may be only a tidier pose.
A support gives something not yet steady a chance to stand.
Having once offered support does not entitle it to declare that whatever it supports must remain dependent on it forever.
There is another detail about the farmer worth noticing.
He works very hard.
The story specifically describes him coming home exhausted and treating his fatigue as evidence that he has helped.
“I've done so much for you” often carries similar force in human relationships.
The more time and energy helpers spend, the more easily they believe their method must be beneficial. Otherwise, all that effort would be difficult to face.
But exhaustion proves only that someone has put a great deal in. It cannot, by itself, prove that the effort went in the right direction.
A person can be extremely diligent about ruining every seedling in a field.
Good intentions are much the same.
They show that an action was not malicious, but cannot exempt it from scrutiny. Especially when someone else bears most of the consequences, how much the helper has given is not the only measure.
We must also ask:
What has the other person gained from this?
What have they lost?
Are they better able to continue from their own resources?
Or can the apparent height be maintained only while we keep intervening?
One of the hardest things to accept about growth is that it cannot appear entirely on an observer's schedule.
We can create conditions, but cannot guarantee the outcome in advance.
We can offer knowledge, but cannot understand on someone else's behalf.
We can make a path easier to enter, but cannot decide for another person whether it is theirs.
This does not make help powerless.
It simply asks the helper to acknowledge that they are not the sole source of growth.

Sometimes our most important contribution is not another visible result, but the protection of a process that has not yet shown itself: keeping premature judgment from flattening it, refusing to turn one slow spell into a verdict of permanent incapacity, and not letting our anxiety set its pace.
This takes more patience than pulling seedlings up, and more judgment than leaving them alone.
Because real care has to do two opposite things at once:
It must not stand idly by when weeding is needed.
It must not reach out and pull the seedlings taller when it is time to wait.
The story of pulling up seedlings does not merely say that faster is not always better.
Its warning is more exacting:
A result can appear ahead of time while the capacity to produce that result is being destroyed.
Looking as though you know how is not the same as being able to do it independently.
Temporary obedience is not the same as understanding.
Moving quickly along a route someone else has arranged does not mean a person has found a direction they want to pursue for themselves.
If help pursues only these visible changes, it may, beneath the appearance of success, take away what growth truly needs.
Seedlings certainly need tending.
But care reaches its fulfillment not when the farmer can finally make them taller on their behalf.
It does so when, one day, he stops touching them, and they can still keep growing from roots of their own.

*Textual basis: the passage beginning “There was a man of Song who, distressed that his seedlings were not growing, pulled them up” in the Mencius, “Gongsun Chou I.” This essay retains the distinction made after the fable between two mistakes: neglecting to weed because one considers care useless, and pulling up seedlings to help them grow. The former abandons care; the latter substitutes outside force for growth.*
